doc.title: Branford Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Why being a musician is cool in New Orleans
summary: No peer pressure against music in New Orleans, where musicians had a tough-guy reputation going back to Jelly Roll Morton and Pops Foster.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Now did you have playmates, or other friends who were also involved in music?

Not involved in music, but, unlike most cities in America, being a musician is cool in New Orleans and the surrounding area. Or, as we say down there, “Oh yeah Bruh, you play that music, huh?” I mean they…. It’s like there’s this whole thing that I saw in movies and had other conversations with…. Like the term “band fag,” I mean I didn’t even know what that was. Some guy, when I was in college, said, “Oh, you know, I was a band fag.” I said, “What’s a band fag?” You know? He said, “Aw, you know, that’s what they call the bands.” Not in New Orleans. That’s not what they call the musicians ‘cause a lot of the musicians in New Orleans were thugs, tough guys. [So…] And this has been…. You can read Jelly Roll Morton’s book. I mean you can hear his oral history and you can read a….
Mr. Jelly Roll, or Pops Foster.

Pops Foster’s book and he talks about how a lot of musicians were cut throats and thugs. So there was a tradition of that in New Orleans and it’s carried over. So the idea of musicians being effeminate, that wasn’t part of my experience growing up. So I didn’t have the same peer pressure that kids from other parts of the country would have had, cause it was cool to play music.
